source_text:
Haec quippe, inquit, in exordio fuerunt duae \'Śubstantiae a se diuisae. et luminis quidem impe* rium tenebat deus pater in sua sancta stirpe perpetuus, in uirtute magnificus, natura ipsa uerus, aeternitate propria semper exultans, continens apud se sapientiam et sensus uitales. per quos etiam duodecim membra luminis sui conprehendit; regni uidelicet proprii diuitias adfluentes. in unoquoque autem membrorum eius sunt recondita milia innumerabilium et inmensorum thesaurorum. ipse uero pater in sua laude praecipuus, magnitudine inconprehensibilis copulata sibi habet beata et gloriosa saecula neque numero neque prolixitate aestimanda, cumquibus idem sanctus atque inlustris pater et genitor degit nullo in regnis eius insignibus aut indigente aut in\'fimo constituto. ita autem fundata sunteiusdem splendidissima regna supra lucidam et beatam terram. ut a nullo umquam aut moueri aut concuti possint.
Haec mihi unde probaturus est, aut haec ipse unde cognouit? noli me terrere paracleti nomine. primo quia non credere incognita, sed certa cognoscere accessi a uobis ipsis factus timidior.
thought_title: Mani's description of the two substances and the land of light
orientation: Augustine has just quoted the opening of Mani's Fundamental Letter, where Mani describes the two eternal substances, and now Augustine challenges Mani to prove these claims.
pass_a_gloss: These [things] indeed, he says, in [the] beginning were two substances from themselves divided. And of [the] light indeed [the] rule was holding God [the] father in his own holy stock perpetual, in virtue magnificent, [by] nature itself true, [by] eternity [his] own always exulting, containing with himself wisdom and senses vital. Through which also [the] twelve members of his light he comprehends; of [the] kingdom namely [his] own riches flowing. In each one however of his members are hidden thousands of innumerable and immeasurable treasures. He himself however [the] father in his own praise preeminent, [in] magnitude incomprehensible joined to himself has blessed and glorious ages neither [by] number nor [by] length to be estimated, with which [ages] the same holy and illustrious father and begetter lives [with] no one in his kingdoms distinguished either lacking or [in a] lowly [position] established. So however are founded of the same most splendid kingdoms upon [the] bright and blessed earth, that by no one ever either to be moved or to be shaken they can. These [things] to me from where is he going to prove, or these [things] he himself from where did he know? Do not terrify me [by] the name of [the] Paraclete. First because not to believe unknown [things], but certain [things] to know I have come to you [pl.] [by] yourselves made more timid.

choices.english: two substances divided from each other
choices.why: Literal rendering of the separation of the two substances, keeping substantia as 'substance' per glossary
rejected: two substances separate from one another
two substances distinct from each other

choices.why: Keeps the adjective 'perpetual' modifying the Father and preserves 'stock' for stirps, which Mani uses for the divine lineage

choices.term: continens apud se sapientiam et sensus uitales
choices.english: containing with himself wisdom and vital senses
choices.why: Literal rendering of continens apud se, emphasizing the Father's possession of these attributes
rejected: holding within himself wisdom and living senses

choices.english: namely the flowing riches of his own kingdom
choices.why: Keeps 'flowing' for adfluentes, suggesting abundance, and 'namely' for uidelicet to mark the explanatory phrase
rejected: that is, the abundant riches of his own kingdom
the overflowing wealth of his own kingdom

choices.why: Renders saecula as 'ages' to preserve the temporal-spatial ambiguity of Mani's myth, rather than 'worlds'

choices.english: Do not frighten me with the name of the Paraclete
choices.why: Keeps the imperative force and the glossary term 'Paraclete' for paracleti
rejected: Do not terrify me by the name of the Paraclete
Do not scare me with the name of the Paraclete

pass_b_english:
"For these," Mani says, "were in the beginning two substances divided from each other. And God the Father held the kingdom of light, perpetual in his holy stock, magnificent in power, true in his very nature, always rejoicing in his own eternity, containing with himself wisdom and vital senses, through which he also comprehends the twelve members of his light—namely, the flowing riches of his own kingdom. And in each one of his members are hidden thousands of innumerable and immeasurable treasures. The Father himself, however, preeminent in his own praise, incomprehensible in greatness, has joined to himself blessed and glorious ages that can be estimated neither by number nor by length, with whom this same holy and illustrious Father and begetter dwells, with no one in his distinguished kingdoms either lacking or placed in a lowly position. And so his most splendid kingdoms are founded upon the bright and blessed land, that they can never be moved or shaken by anyone."

How is he going to prove these things to me, or how did he himself come to know them? Do not frighten me with the name of the Paraclete. First, because I came to you not to believe unknown things but to know certain things, having been made more timid by you yourselves.

last_rejected.quote: having been made more timid by you yourselves
last_rejected.why: "timidior" means more fearful/afraid, not more timid; and the causal sense is adversative (despite/because of you I came), not result.
last_rejected.fix: made all the more fearful by you yourselves
last_rejected.ruling: "Timid" is within timidior's normal range; causal sense is defensible, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: "Noli" + infinitive is a negative command/prohibition ("Do not try to frighten me" or "Don't you dare frighten me"), not a simple request.
last_rejected.fix: Don't try to frighten me with the name of the Paraclete.
last_rejected.ruling: "Do not frighten me" correctly renders noli + infinitive as prohibition; no meaning lost.
